extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners studying misinformation, social/information network analysts, public-health communicators and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A research paper presenting a three-tier analytical framework, dataset, and empirical analyses to study how conspiracy theories, fake remedies, and false reports about COVID-19 emerge and propagate on digital platforms. The work aims to inform targeted interventions and policy/health-communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-tier analytical framework (motive analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presents a structured, three-tier analytical framework that investigates how multiple motives - including fear, politics, and profit - can lead to a misleading claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze and categorize the underlying motives (e.g., fear, political incentives, profit-seeking) that give rise to misinformation as part of a systematic framework for understanding origin and drivers of misleading claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative structure analysis (thematic elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizes the importance of narrative structures, systematically identifying and quantifying the thematic elements that drive conspiracy theories, fake remedies, and false reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify, code, and quantify narrative/thematic components in misinformation (e.g., typical storylines, motifs) to understand what drives spread and belief; use systematic, quantitative methods rather than anecdotal description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source analysis (roles of different actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presents a comprehensive analysis of different sources of misinformation, highlighting the varied roles played by individuals, state-based organizations, media outlets, and other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish and evaluate the contributions and behaviors of different source types (individuals, state actors, media outlets, etc.) to capture heterogeneity in origins and propagation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset composition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A dataset of 5,614 posts on the internet that contained misinformation about COVID-19 was used for this study; these posts were published in 2020 on 427 online sources from 193 countries and in 49 languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize breadth and diversity in data (size, number of sources, geographic and linguistic coverage) to support generalizable analyses; report dataset provenance, time window, and composition explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications for public policy and health communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Discusses multiple potential implications of these findings for public policy and health communication, illustrating how insights gained from motive, narrative, and source analyses can guide more targeted interventions in the context of misinformation detection on digital platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate analytic findings into actionable recommendations for policy and communication interventions; demonstrate how motive/narrative/source insights inform targeted remediation or detection strategies.
